title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS TREAT STRANGERS LIKE JESUS… BUT TREAT THEIR OWN SPOUSES LIKE ENEMIES?
paragraphs: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS TREAT STRANGERS LIKE JESUS… BUT TREAT THEIR OWN SPOUSES LIKE ENEMIES?

They can pray for a stranger, forgive a church member, and speak gently to everyone outside their home. But the person they promised to love before God is quietly breaking under the weight of their words. What happens when your public Christianity looks more like Christ than your private marriage?
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't leave bruises.
It doesn't make the evening news. It doesn't always end in divorce. Sometimes it sits quietly at the dinner table, wearing a wedding ring, pretending everything is fine.
And perhaps the most painful part?
The person causing that heartbreak might be someone everybody else calls a wonderful Christian.
Someone who serves at church. Someone who knows Scripture. Someone who can spend an hour comforting a struggling friend but cannot spare five minutes to listen to the person sleeping beside them.
Someone who says, “God bless you,” to strangers with genuine warmth, then walks through the front door and speaks to their spouse as though kindness is a privilege they no longer deserve.
And the spouse?
They hear the laughter from the other room.
They watch their husband or wife answer a friend's phone call with enthusiasm after ignoring their own attempts to talk all evening.
They see the patience. The tenderness. The compassion.
They know that person is capable of being gentle.
That is what makes it hurt so much.
Because sometimes the deepest wound in a marriage isn't discovering that your spouse doesn't know how to love.
It's discovering that they know exactly how to show kindness.
They just seem to have stopped showing it to you.
And before you assume this article is about your husband or your wife, there is a question every married Christian needs the courage to ask.
What if the person who needs to repent isn't sitting across from you?
What if that person is reading these words right now?
Somewhere tonight, a woman is lying beside a man who spent Sunday morning lifting his hands in worship, yet hasn't spoken tenderly to her in weeks.
Somewhere else, a husband is sitting alone after another evening of being belittled, wondering why the woman who encourages everybody at church seems to have nothing encouraging left for him.
And somewhere, a couple who once prayed for God to bring them together now barely know how to pray together without feeling the distance between them.
Their marriage didn't necessarily collapse in one terrible moment.
It happened in ordinary moments.
A sarcastic comment.
An apology withheld.
A conversation interrupted.
A private humiliation disguised as a joke.
A tired spouse asking for affection and receiving irritation instead.
One person saying, “Can we please talk?”
And the other answering, “Not this again.”
Little by little, the home that was supposed to be a place of refuge became a place where somebody learned to measure every word before speaking.
And then Sunday comes.
The smiles return.
The greetings become warm.
The Bible opens.
The prayers sound beautiful.
But God sees Monday too.
And the Jesus we worship in public is the same Jesus who sees how we treat one another behind closed doors.
This is where Scripture becomes painfully personal.
In Ephesians 4:32, the apostle Paul writes:
Look carefully at the word translated “kind.”
In the Greek text, Paul uses χρηστοί (chrēstoí), meaning kind, benevolent, or gracious in one's treatment of others.
Then comes εὔσπλαγχνοι (eúsplanchnoi), commonly translated “tenderhearted,” conveying deep compassion.
Paul is not describing a polished public personality.
He is describing the kind of character that should grow in people who have received the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And notice something else.
He does not say, “Be kind to one another, except when you have been married for fifteen years.”
He does not say, “Be tenderhearted toward people who appreciate you.”
He does not say, “Forgive the church members, but keep a permanent record of your spouse's failures.”
The command is not suspended at the front door of your house.
If anything, the intimacy of marriage makes its application even more urgent.
Because the person who sees your weaknesses most closely should not automatically receive the least compassion.
Yet why does this happen?
Why can a Christian show extraordinary patience to a stranger and extraordinary impatience toward the person they married?
Sometimes it is because strangers encounter our presentation, while spouses encounter our patterns.
A stranger may see us for five minutes.
Our spouse sees us when we're exhausted, disappointed, frightened, financially pressured, or struggling with something we haven't surrendered to God.
Strangers rarely confront the unresolved wounds in our character.
Marriage often does.
A stranger doesn't usually remind us of an argument from three years ago.
A stranger doesn't know the promises we broke.
A stranger doesn't ask why we keep avoiding difficult conversations.
But a spouse might.
And when pride is stronger than humility, we may respond to that closeness not with gratitude, but with defensiveness.
Sometimes familiarity becomes an excuse for carelessness.
We begin to assume that the person who has stayed will always stay.
We stop saying thank you.
We stop noticing sacrifices.
We offer strangers the benefit of the doubt while interpreting our spouse's every mistake through the lens of past disappointment.
We become polite where we want approval and careless where we assume acceptance.
But love that only behaves beautifully when people are watching needs serious examination.
Jesus spoke directly to the danger of outward religious appearance without inward transformation.
In Matthew 23:27–28, He rebuked religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
That passage was not specifically about marriage, and we should not pretend that it was.
But its warning reaches into every place where outward religious reputation becomes a substitute for genuine obedience.
You can protect your Christian image and still neglect your Christian character.
You can defend biblical marriage in public while failing to practice biblical love in private.
You can know the language of grace and still refuse to extend it.
And if that realization stings, don't rush to defend yourself.
Ask the Holy Spirit to show you what needs to change.
Because conviction is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes conviction is the doorway through which we finally stop running from the truth.
There is another passage that deserves our attention.
Colossians 3:19 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.” (KJV)
The Greek expression μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikraínesthe) carries the sense of not becoming embittered or harsh toward them.
Think about that.
The Holy Spirit, through Paul, addressed the danger of bitterness entering the marriage relationship.
Not merely adultery.
Not merely abandonment.
Bitterness.
That slow poison that turns ordinary conversations into battles.
That habit of responding sharply because resentment has been rehearsed for too long.
That coldness that grows when offenses are collected instead of honestly addressed.
And husbands, this command is not permission to demand submission while withholding tenderness.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
The Greek verb ἀγαπᾶτε (agapâte) comes from agapaō, meaning to love. In this context, Paul defines that love by pointing to Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Not domination.
Not intimidation.
Not emotional abandonment.
Not using Scripture to win arguments.
Christlike marital love is sacrificial.
It does not ask, “How much can I demand from this person?”
It asks, “How can I honor Christ in the way I care for this person?”
And wives are not exempt from the call to kindness, respect, and faithful love.
Ephesians 5:21 calls believers to submit to one another in the fear of God, and the surrounding passage gives particular instructions for husbands and wives.
Whatever theological differences Christians may have about the application of marital roles, Scripture gives no spouse permission to be cruel, contemptuous, manipulative, or abusive.
A marriage is not made holy by one person having power over another.
A marriage honors God when His truth shapes how both people live.
And this is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because some Christians have confused being respected with being feared.
They say, “My spouse needs to respect me.”
But what they actually demand is silence.
They say, “I'm the head of this household.”
But they use that claim to avoid accountability.
They say, “The Bible says to forgive.”
But what they mean is, “Stop bringing up what I did, even though I haven't changed.”
Others use tears, guilt, withdrawal, or public embarrassment to control the person they promised to cherish.
And some hide behind religious language so effectively that their spouses begin to question whether asking for basic dignity is somehow unspiritual.
It is not.
Forgiveness is biblical. So are repentance, truthfulness, accountability, and justice.
Reconciliation is not the same thing as pretending nothing happened.
Trust is not automatically restored because somebody said sorry.
And the call to love your spouse never requires you to accept violence, coercion, threats, or ongoing abuse.
If you are unsafe, seeking protection and qualified help is not a failure of faith.
God's Word must never be turned into a weapon that traps someone in harm.
Now consider a quieter form of marital pain.
Not every wounded marriage is marked by dramatic cruelty.
Sometimes the tragedy is neglect.
Two people who still love each other but have forgotten how to communicate that love.
They pay the bills.
They raise the children.
They attend church.
They fulfill their responsibilities.
But affection has become rare.
Every conversation is about schedules, expenses, responsibilities, or problems.
Nobody asks, “How is your heart?”
Nobody says, “I noticed you've been carrying a lot lately.”
Nobody reaches across the distance because both are waiting for the other to move first.
And perhaps neither person intended to become this way.
Life became exhausting.
Parenthood became overwhelming.
Financial pressure swallowed their attention.
Disappointments accumulated.
Unspoken hurt turned into emotional distance.
Then distance became routine.
And routine began to feel permanent.
But what if permanent is not the word God wants written over your story?
What if this is the moment He is inviting you to stop treating your marriage as something that merely survives and begin treating your spouse as someone worth loving intentionally?
Remember how it began.
There may have been a time when a single message from that person could change your entire day.
You waited for their calls.
You listened to stories you'd already heard because hearing their voice mattered more than the story itself.
You noticed their favorite food.
You remembered the little things.
You prayed about your future.
You imagined growing old together.
And on your wedding day, you made promises before God.
Not promises to feel romantic every morning.
Not promises that neither of you would ever fail.
But promises of covenant faithfulness.
Promises that love would become more than an emotion.
So what happened to the tenderness?
Where did the patience go?
When did the person you once thanked God for become the person you speak to most carelessly?
Perhaps the answer isn't that all love has disappeared.
Perhaps love has been buried beneath pride, exhaustion, resentment, disappointment, or wounds neither of you has learned to address.
And perhaps the next faithful step is not another argument about who started it.
Perhaps it is a moment of humility.
“I know I have hurt you.”
“I have been kinder to other people than I have been to you.”
“I have made you feel alone.”
“I have defended myself when I should have listened.”
“I cannot undo those moments, but I want to repent and begin changing.”
Those words will not instantly heal years of pain.
They are not magic.
And an apology without changed behavior can become another wound.
But genuine repentance has a different sound from self-defense.
Self-defense says, “You made me act this way.”
Repentance says, “I am responsible for how I responded.”
Self-defense says, “Why can't you just move on?”
Repentance says, “I understand why rebuilding trust may take time.”
Self-defense says, “Nobody's perfect.”
Repentance says, “Lord, show me what I need to surrender.”
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a message we preach.
It becomes the power by which we are called to live.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus proclaims:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeîte) means “repent,” calling for a change of mind and direction in response to God's kingdom.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
It is admitting that the old way cannot remain the accepted way.
And the good news is that Jesus does not call sinners to repentance while offering no mercy.
He came to save sinners.
He bore sin at the cross.
He rose again.
He offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
That does not mean every marriage will be restored or every wounded relationship will become safe.
But it means no one has to defend sin as though transformation were impossible.
The Gospel gives us a reason to stop hiding.
Because the Savior who knows the truth about us is also the Savior who calls us to come into the light.
Think of the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood publicly exposed, surrounded by accusers.
Jesus refused to join their condemnation, and He did not treat her sin as meaningless.
He told her, “Go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy and holiness were not enemies in His response.
That matters for our marriages.
Grace is not permission to keep wounding somebody.
Grace invites us out of the very patterns that have wounded them.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been living under the weight of shame.
You know you've been harsh.
You know you've neglected your spouse.
You know the smile you give the congregation doesn't always match the attitude you bring home.
You love Jesus, but you have been resisting His correction in this part of your life.
Hear this carefully.
Your failure does not need to become your final identity.
But neither should you use God's forgiveness as an excuse to remain unchanged.
Confess what is true.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
Listen without immediately correcting your spouse's account of their pain.
Make room for accountability.
If the wounds run deep, seek help from a qualified Christian marriage counselor who understands healthy relationships and safety.
If you have been controlling or abusive, take responsibility and seek specialized intervention; do not pressure your spouse into joint counseling or reconciliation.
Let repentance become visible in consistent actions, not only emotional promises.
And if you're the spouse who has been carrying the hurt, please understand something equally important.
You are not responsible for manufacturing another person's repentance.
You cannot love somebody into taking accountability.
You cannot pray hard enough to make someone else choose honesty.
You can pray.
You can seek wisdom.
You can establish boundaries.
You can ask for support.
You can refuse to repay cruelty with cruelty.
But you do not have to deny reality in order to honor God.
Jesus Christ sees the wounds nobody at church knows about.
And He is not impressed by religious appearances that conceal mistreatment.
One of the most revealing passages about Christian love appears in 1 Corinthians 13:4–5:

“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.” (KJV)
The word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη (agápē), love.
And the Greek expression χρηστεύεται (chrēsteúetai) means “is kind” or “acts kindly.”
Love is not merely something we claim to possess.
It expresses itself in how we treat people.
Especially when we're tired.
Especially when we disagree.
Especially when the person standing before us knows our weaknesses.
Especially when there is no audience to applaud our patience.
Imagine what might change if Christian husbands and wives began measuring spiritual maturity not only by how faithfully they attended church, but also by how faithfully they practiced love at home.
Imagine a husband who stops mid-argument and says, “I was speaking harshly. I'm sorry. You deserve to be heard.”
Imagine a wife who recognizes that sarcasm has become her shield and chooses an honest conversation instead.
Imagine two exhausted parents who turn off their phones for fifteen minutes and ask each other how they're really doing.
Imagine a couple who have avoided praying together for months finally sitting side by side, unsure what to say, and beginning with:
“Lord, help us.”
Not an impressive prayer.
Not a performance.
Just two people acknowledging their need for grace.
Sometimes that is where the first honest conversation begins.
Not with a perfect speech.
Not with an instant miracle.
But with humility.
With listening.
With the willingness to stop repeating what has been destroying the relationship.
And if you are single, please don't dismiss this message as something only married people need.
The character you cultivate today is the character you carry into your closest relationships tomorrow.
Kindness is not something you should begin practicing after a wedding.
It is part of following Christ now.
And if you are divorced, widowed, separated, or recovering from a deeply painful marriage, this message is not meant to place shame on your shoulders.
Your life is not spiritually worthless because your marriage ended.
Your identity is not reduced to your relationship status.
The Gospel is larger than marital success.
Jesus is the Savior of sinners, the comforter of the brokenhearted, and the Lord who calls His people to walk in truth.
If your spouse described the way you treat them when nobody is watching, would that description resemble the Jesus you tell other people about?
Not the version of you who shakes hands at church.
Not the version who comments “Amen” under Christian posts.
Not the version who knows the right Bible verses.
The version who comes home exhausted.
The version who responds when challenged.
The version who speaks when frustrated.
The version who handles another person's vulnerability.
Would they say you are gentle?
Would they say you listen?
Would they say your apologies lead to change?
Would they say your faith makes them feel safer, more valued, and more respected?
Or would they quietly admit that the people outside your home receive the kindness they have been longing for?
This question is not about achieving perfection.
Every marriage has difficult moments.
Every Christian still needs grace.
But we must never confuse imperfection with permission to remain unrepentant.
In James 1:22, Scripture says:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” (KJV)
We can hear sermons about love for years and still resist the daily practice of loving.
We can memorize verses about forgiveness and remain unwilling to acknowledge our own offenses.
We can share inspirational posts while ignoring the person asking us to put down the phone and listen.
And yes, even this article can become another religious message we agree with without allowing it to change us.
Please don't let that happen.
If you recognize yourself in these words, don't simply send the article to your spouse as proof that they are wrong.
Begin by asking what God may be showing you.
If appropriate and safe, go to the person you've hurt.
Not to deliver another sermon.
Not to explain why your behavior was understandable.
But to listen.
To confess.
To make things right where you can.
And to demonstrate change over time.
Because the goal is not to win a biblical argument.
The goal is to become more like Jesus.
You don't have to expose your spouse, reveal private details, or tell the internet something that could put you at risk.
But perhaps you can write:
And if you feel exhausted from fighting for what is right, perhaps your simple response is:
“Pray for me.”
Those few words may become the beginning of an honest conversation with God.
They may also remind another believer reading silently that they are not alone.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ changed the way you love, forgive, communicate, or take responsibility, consider sharing it.
Somebody needs to know that repentance can produce real change.
Not every story ends with reconciliation.
But transformation through Jesus Christ is real, and every testimony of His faithfulness deserves to point back to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish another Christian article that makes people emotional for a moment.
Not to gather applause for religious language.
But to keep bringing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Because some people have nobody helping them understand the Bible.
Some are struggling in marriages they cannot openly discuss.
Some are trying to rebuild their faith after years of disappointment.
Some are new believers who desperately need sound biblical teaching.
Others have spent decades in church but are only now beginning to recognize the difference between religious activity and genuine discipleship.
They need more than another passing inspirational quote.
They need the Word of God.
They need encouragement rooted in truth.
They need opportunities to grow.
And they need to be reminded, again and again, that Jesus Christ is worthy of following in the ordinary, unseen places of life.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Gospel more clearly, strengthen their faith, and become more intentional disciples of Jesus Christ.
And we want that mission to continue reaching people who may never walk through the doors of our churches.
People scrolling through Facebook at two in the morning because their hearts are heavy.
People questioning whether God can forgive them.
People whose marriages are hurting.
People who need biblical truth presented with both courage and compassion.
But meaningful ministry also requires time, resources, and people willing to stand behind the mission.
Your first responsibility is to give faithfully, wisely, and willingly according to biblical conviction, while caring for the responsibilities God has entrusted to you.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
We want people who genuinely believe in what Gospel Warrior is doing and desire to help that work continue.
These items are simply ways to encourage faith, share meaningful messages, and help sustain the work.
They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is the reason.
The Gospel is the message.
Changed lives are the prayer.
Not because we need another number on a screen.
But because someone in your circle may be silently living through the very pain we have been discussing.
A husband may need to confront his harshness.
A wife may need to recognize how resentment has shaped her words.
A struggling couple may need encouragement to seek help.
Someone who has been mistreated may need to hear that biblical love never requires them to accept abuse.
And someone who has been hiding behind a Christian reputation may finally need to face the truth about their private character.
Not as a trophy of how much you agree with it.
For the day exhaustion makes gentleness difficult.
For the day you need to remember that Christian maturity is not proven only in public worship.
Sometimes it is revealed in the quiet decisions nobody applauds.
Our prayer is that you will keep opening your Bible, seeking Christ, growing in truth, and allowing His Word to shape the way you live.
Because one day, the applause of strangers will fade.
The compliments from church members will fade.
The public recognition will fade.
But the words you spoke at home may remain in somebody's memory for years.
May those memories increasingly become memories of grace.
Of humility.
Of repentance.
Of tenderness.
Of a husband who learned to listen.
Of a wife who chose honesty over contempt.
Of two imperfect people who stopped pretending and began seeking help.
Of a wounded person who found safety, support, and hope.
Of a home where the name of Jesus was not merely spoken, but honored through the way people treated one another.
And if your marriage is already deeply wounded, don't hear this as a demand to manufacture a beautiful ending.
Hear it as an invitation to bring the truth into the light and take the next faithful step before God.
Some stories need reconciliation.
Some need protection and distance.
Some need professional help.
All need truth.
And every one of us needs the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps the most unforgettable scandal is not that Christians sometimes fail to love perfectly.
It is that we can become so skilled at looking loving to the world that we forget to love the people closest to us.
But the Gospel calls us to something better.
Not image management.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
A life surrendered to Christ.
A heart willing to repent.
A faith that bears fruit.
A love that learns to be kind when nobody is watching.
Because the real test of your Christianity may not be how warmly you greet the stranger after Sunday worship.
It may be how gently you speak to the person waiting for you when you get home.
Don't let the person who knows your love most intimately become the person who has to watch everyone else receive it.
